text_paragraph_1: Democracy in Africa has faced considerable challenges over the past decade. According  to the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy (Skaaning, 2021), while most of the democracies  surveyed by Afrobarometer a decade ago have maintained democratic rule, several have  experienced democratic backsliding in the years since to “multiparty autocracies” (Benin,  Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania) or military regimes (Burkina  Faso, Madagascar, and Mali). Only one country has improved its position, as Zambia  returned to “electoral democracy” status in 2021 (Herre, Rodés-Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina,  2026a; France24, 2026). As measured by V-Dem’s (2026) indices of liberal democracy, many  other countries have experienced declines in the quality of electoral contestation and political freedoms over the same period (Herre, Rodés Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina, 2026b).
text_paragraph_2: These developments raise the question: How hungry are ordinary Africans  for democracy?
text_paragraph_3: Since its inception, Afrobarometer’s surveys have contained sets of questions that measure the extent to which people want to live in a democratically governed society (or what we call “demand for democracy”) and the  degree to which they believe they are living in a democracy (what we have termed the  perceived “supply of democracy”).

FAO and UNOSSC mark United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation with joint event on Global South solutions
text_paragraph_1: FAO Director-General highlights practical solutions ahead of UN Day
text_paragraph_2: FAO Director-General QU Dongyu, center, with the South-South Cooperation team in Gayaza.
text_paragraph_3: Rome – This year’s United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation , 12 September, highlights FAO projects that show how collaboration among countries of the Global South can scale practical solutions for the transformation of agrifood systems. The Global South comprises 134 countries that are home to 80 percent of the world’s population, nearly half of global trade in goods and more than 40 percent of global economic output. Meanwhile, South-South trade has reached almost $7 trillion a year, and foreign direct investment flows among developing countries have quadrupled since the 1990s. Across the UN system, South-South and Triangular Cooperation is being positioned not as a stand-alone area of work but as a strategic means of implementing nationally owned Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) priorities. Reductions in official development assistance from traditional donors are placing greater pressure on development financing, making South-South and Triangular Cooperation an increasingly important mechanism to mobilize knowledge, technical expertise, and funding for sustainable impact. “South-South and Triangular Cooperation is one of FAO’s most effective programmes for delivery,” according to Director-General QU Dongyu . FAO’s catalytic role FAO’s work on South-South and Triangular Cooperation ( SSTC ) reflects the spirit of “Solidarity Rising,” helping farmers, experts, researchers and institutions – the holders of practical knowledge – exchange experiences on climate-smart agriculture, water management, digital agriculture, animal health, food safety and sustainable value chains. “Many of the innovations needed are already being used successfully in countries facing similar production challenges,” FAO Director-General QU Dongyu said. South-South Cooperation makes a difference as “it provides a practical way to move solutions faster – by sharing technologies and experience, and adapting them to local conditions,” he emphasised. It is “more than just a cooperation modality – it is a strategic instrument for transformation,” he added . Over the past two decades, thousands of experts have shared their expertise in more than 90 countries through FAO’s South-South and Triangular Cooperation ( SSTC ) Programme. South-South Cooperation is a natural and increasingly important approach, building on peer-to-peer exchange and the increasing economic footprint of developing countries. It is also emerging as a critical source of innovation, showing the Global South is not only a beneficiary of development cooperation but also a source of practical solutions. To support FAO’s mandate to bolster global food security, agricultural productivity and resilience, South-South cooperation also draws on farmers’ deep practical knowledge, especially in tropical regions, where local experience can provide insights not readily available in more temperate regions. Since the late 1970s, FAO has recognised the importance of SSTC, which also harnesses traditional donors, international financial institutions, the private sector, academia, and other partners. This work has mobilized more than $550 million in initiatives to date, with major contributions from China, Brazil, and Türkiye. The FAO-China South-South Cooperation Programme is a clear example of SSTC in practice. Since 2010, the Programme has combined field-level demonstrations, research collaboration, policy support, and institutional partnerships, allowing it to operate at the community, national, and global levels and helping results endure beyond a single project cycle. The Government of China has contributed a total of $130 million to support the implementation of three phases of the Programme, which has supported 39 projects, deployed more than 340 long-term experts to support developing countries, and reached millions of people directly and indirectly. The FAO-Republic of Korea partnership also exemplifies triangular cooperation in action. The project facilitated the transfer and adaptation of innovative rice production practices in Tanzania, Côte d’Ivoire, and the Philippines. Through joint research, capacity development and policy dialogue, this collaboration supported national institutions, improved knowledge exchange among countries of the Global South, and promoted sustainable technologies. This alliance demonstrates how triangular cooperation can draw on the comparative advantages of diverse partners to scale sustainable agrifood solutions and deliver practical development results. Together, these examples underscore the role of the Global South as a driver of innovation and solutions for agrifood systems transformation – supporting better production, better nutrition, a better environment, and a better life, leaving no one behind.

PP106: Democracy: Faltering demand in Africa?
text_paragraph_1: Democracy in Africa has faced considerable challenges over the past decade. According  to the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy (Skaaning, 2021), while most of the democracies  surveyed by Afrobarometer a decade ago have maintained democratic rule, several have  experienced democratic backsliding in the years since to “multiparty autocracies” (Benin,  Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania) or military regimes (Burkina  Faso, Madagascar, and Mali). Only one country has improved its position, as Zambia  returned to “electoral democracy” status in 2021 (Herre, Rodés-Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina,  2026a; France24, 2026). As measured by V-Dem’s (2026) indices of liberal democracy, many  other countries have experienced declines in the quality of electoral contestation and political freedoms over the same period (Herre, Rodés Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina, 2026b).
text_paragraph_2: These developments raise the question: How hungry are ordinary Africans  for democracy?
text_paragraph_3: Since its inception, Afrobarometer’s surveys have contained sets of questions that measure the extent to which people want to live in a democratically governed society (or what we call “demand for democracy”) and the  degree to which they believe they are living in a democracy (what we have termed the  perceived “supply of democracy”).

Jordan generates around 10.9 million tonnes of animal waste annually, while Egypt produces approximately 44–45 million tonnes of agricultural waste, including 42.4 million tonnes of crop residues. title: Earth From Orbit Is Unpredictable and Messy. Could 'Liquid' AI Clear the View?
text_paragraph_1: Monitoring Earth from above is a messy, inconsistent business. Clouds can block a satellite view, the angle of the Sun can create huge shadows, and orbital paths might not take a system across the same general area for weeks. That inconsistency is hard to deal with for traditional software, and can even confuse standard deep learning algorithms. But, according to a new review paper, available in pre-print by researchers Raul-Alexandru Gorgan and Dorian Gorgan of the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, there’s a new type of frontier AI that could be able to help - bio-inspired Liquid Neural Networks.
text_paragraph_2: Modern society relies heavily on Earth observation, but collecting data in a meaningful way that is understandable to a deep learning system is complicated. For example, most deep learning networks, such as those that drive autonomous cars, expect data points to come in at regular intervals, and usually for those intervals to be relatively short, so that small changes can be distinguished and used to inform the model.
text_paragraph_3: That level of regularity doesn’t happen in Earth observation. The most obvious culprit is clouds. Satellites in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) can have their views of certain areas over the planet blocked by clouds - repeatedly in many cases. Combine that with relatively erratic flyover schedules, and some satellites can go over a month between being able to take pictures of certain parts of the world.

text_paragraph_1: Democracy in Africa has faced considerable challenges over the past decade. According  to the Lexical Index of Electoral Democracy (Skaaning, 2021), while most of the democracies  surveyed by Afrobarometer a decade ago have maintained democratic rule, several have  experienced democratic backsliding in the years since to “multiparty autocracies” (Benin,  Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania) or military regimes (Burkina  Faso, Madagascar, and Mali). Only one country has improved its position, as Zambia  returned to “electoral democracy” status in 2021 (Herre, Rodés-Guirao, & Ortiz-Ospina,  2026a; France24, 2026). text_paragraph_1: Babagana Ahmadu , the Representative of the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Pretoria, recently died on a flight to Newark en route to Atlanta. Unlike many overcautious UN bureaucrats who unconsciously cut the figure of a “glorified nobody,” Babagana was a man of passion and ideas who also ran a farm in his volatile northeastern Nigerian hometown of Maiduguri. He was a practical man who literally liked to get his hands dirty. Before coming to South Africa in 2023, in an 18-year career, Babagana had been FAO Representative in Namibia, Gambia, and Sudan: fittingly for a dyed-in-the wool Pan-African, he had covered Southern, West, and Eastern Africa. In Addis Ababa – the capital of African diplomacy – he also worked as the first ever Director for Rural Economy and Agriculture in the African Union (AU) Commission under the leadership of former Malian president, Alpha Konaré (2003-2007). Babagana’s dedicated service to FAO in Gambia was acknowledged when he was awarded the Insignia of Commander of the National Order of the Republic on his departure in 2013, with the country’s leader, Yahya Jammeh, also praising his “unprecedented” achievements during his five-year tenure.
text_paragraph_2: Tirelessly traversing rural communities in Gambia, Babagana sought particularly to build infrastructure to support sustainable vegetation production; to increase the productive capacity of women farmers in vegetable farming and fish processing; and to improve storage facilities. In Sudan, he prioritised food security, climate change, and alleviating the deleterious impacts of internal conflicts, at a time, in 2022, when FAO was providing life-saving assistance to more than 2.5 million vulnerable Sudanese.
text_paragraph_3: His main concern was always the most vulnerable groups: women, children, herders, and rural farmers who struggled to acquire funding, technologies, markets, and agricultural inputs.

text_paragraph_1: Industrial policy can only succeed with both sustained political commitment and abundant, reliable energy. Liberia has the political will but needs to resolve its power question. A new injection of grant funds from the Millennium Challenge Corporation is an opportunity to link Liberia’s industrialization ambitions in rubber and iron ore with meaningful, timely, debt-free investments in Liberia’s power sector. The Government of Liberia should use this grant funding where it is most needed — transmission and utility reform — to leverage additional generation, whether through private investment or the West African Power Pool. This critical confluence can kickstart Liberia’s economic growth and job creation, if it can take advantage of the moment.
text_paragraph_2: To effectively execute on industrial policy, a country needs many things. This memo focuses on two of the most important: sustained political commitment and abundant, reliable energy. Liberia offers an instructive case study of when you have the will but lack the power.
text_paragraph_3: Over the past two administrations, Liberia has demonstrated an unusual degree of political continuity around industrial policy. Former President George Weah’s Executive Order 124 prohibited the export of unprocessed natural rubber. Current President Joseph Boakai subsequently extended the policy through Executive Order 151. Across party lines, the government has maintained a consistent objective: move Liberia away from raw commodity exports and toward domestic processing and value addition, starting with rubber (Liberia’s largest export crop). That consensus solves one of the most difficult problems in industrial development — political continuity and predictability. The next challenge is more practical: whether Liberia’s energy system can support the industrialization the nation seeks.

text_paragraph_1: Africa is too wide to be summarized as a single market, and that’s a common mistake made by many, especially in the northern hemisphere. However, one aspect of solar in Africa applies to the entire continent: its tremendous solar resource. From the desertic areas of the Sahara to the savanna zones in the south and the lush forests in its center, Africa is never short of solar energy but struggles to deploy PV as fast as other continents. The reasons are multiple, from incumbents to financing limitations, from skills to the lack of political willingness (but this is changing fast). But PV development is accelerating beyond the 20 GW installed at the end of 2025, and the reason is not only the need to acceleration electrification rate, but the tremendous impact of rising oil and gas prices.
text_paragraph_2: The case of Madagascar will be discussed here: an island nation in the Indian Ocean, faces one of the most severe energy crises in Africa. With an extremely low electrification rate (depending on the interpretation of numbers, as little as 14% of the population could be considered electrified), most of its population relies on a mix of hydropower systems and diesel generators—a costly and unsustainable solution. The high price of oil, compounded by logistical challenges in transporting fuel across the country’s rugged terrain, has made electricity prohibitively expensive. Main local utility Jirama operates at a loss, as government-imposed price caps prevent them from passing the full cost of generation onto consumers. The result? Electricity is frequently rationed, with many communities experiencing blackouts for several hours each day.
text_paragraph_3: Political unrest at the end of 2025, that led to the exile of the former president André Rajoelina and a temporary takeover by the army was driven by recurring rolling blackouts, as well as water shortages, managed by the very same utility. While we won’t focus on the latest, aging infrastructure and uncompetitive electricity costs are a permanent burden for minority of the population with access to electricity.

text_paragraph_1: FAO Director-General highlights practical solutions ahead of UN Day
text_paragraph_2: FAO Director-General QU Dongyu, center, with the South-South Cooperation team in Gayaza.
text_paragraph_3: Rome – This year’s United Nations Day for South-South Cooperation , 12 September, highlights FAO projects that show how collaboration among countries of the Global South can scale practical solutions for the transformation of agrifood systems. The Global South comprises 134 countries that are home to 80 percent of the world’s population, nearly half of global trade in goods and more than 40 percent of global economic output. Meanwhile, South-South trade has reached almost $7 trillion a year, and foreign direct investment flows among developing countries have quadrupled since the 1990s. Across the UN system, South-South and Triangular Cooperation is being positioned not as a stand-alone area of work but as a strategic means of implementing nationally owned Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) priorities. Reductions in official development assistance from traditional donors are placing greater pressure on development financing, making South-South and Triangular Cooperation an increasingly important mechanism to mobilize knowledge, technical expertise, and funding for sustainable impact. “South-South and Triangular Cooperation is one of FAO’s most effective programmes for delivery,” according to Director-General QU Dongyu . FAO’s catalytic role FAO’s work on South-South and Triangular Cooperation ( SSTC ) reflects the spirit of “Solidarity Rising,” helping farmers, experts, researchers and institutions – the holders of practical knowledge – exchange experiences on climate-smart agriculture, water management, digital agriculture, animal health, food safety and sustainable value chains. “Many of the innovations needed are already being used successfully in countries facing similar production challenges,” FAO Director-General QU Dongyu said. South-South Cooperation makes a difference as “it provides a practical way to move solutions faster – by sharing technologies and experience, and adapting them to local conditions,” he emphasised. It is “more than just a cooperation modality – it is a strategic instrument for transformation,” he added . Over the past two decades, thousands of experts have shared their expertise in more than 90 countries through FAO’s South-South and Triangular Cooperation ( SSTC ) Programme. South-South Cooperation is a natural and increasingly important approach, building on peer-to-peer exchange and the increasing economic footprint of developing countries. It is also emerging as a critical source of innovation, showing the Global South is not only a beneficiary of development cooperation but also a source of practical solutions. To support FAO’s mandate to bolster global food security, agricultural productivity and resilience, South-South cooperation also draws on farmers’ deep practical knowledge, especially in tropical regions, where local experience can provide insights not readily available in more temperate regions. Since the late 1970s, FAO has recognised the importance of SSTC, which also harnesses traditional donors, international financial institutions, the private sector, academia, and other partners. This work has mobilized more than $550 million in initiatives to date, with major contributions from China, Brazil, and Türkiye. The FAO-China South-South Cooperation Programme is a clear example of SSTC in practice. Since 2010, the Programme has combined field-level demonstrations, research collaboration, policy support, and institutional partnerships, allowing it to operate at the community, national, and global levels and helping results endure beyond a single project cycle. The Government of China has contributed a total of $130 million to support the implementation of three phases of the Programme, which has supported 39 projects, deployed more than 340 long-term experts to support developing countries, and reached millions of people directly and indirectly. The FAO-Republic of Korea partnership also exemplifies triangular cooperation in action. The project facilitated the transfer and adaptation of innovative rice production practices in Tanzania, Côte d’Ivoire, and the Philippines. Through joint research, capacity development and policy dialogue, this collaboration supported national institutions, improved knowledge exchange among countries of the Global South, and promoted sustainable technologies. This alliance demonstrates how triangular cooperation can draw on the comparative advantages of diverse partners to scale sustainable agrifood solutions and deliver practical development results. Together, these examples underscore the role of the Global South as a driver of innovation and solutions for agrifood systems transformation – supporting better production, better nutrition, a better environment, and a better life, leaving no one behind.

text_paragraph_1: By Dharamraj Deenoo To ICT/BPO Experts  of Mauritius, Guardians of Renewal and Dignity, The closure of Concentrix has sent shockwaves through our ICT/BPO sector. For many, it feels like a blow to one of our most trusted engines of employment and foreign exchange. Yet let us be clear: this is not the collapse of an industry, but the warning signal of a deeper structural shift. Mauritius can no longer compete merely as a low‑cost call‑centre destination. The world has changed, and so must we. The real danger is to cling to yesterday’s model. The real opportunity is to build tomorrow’s industry. Mauritius must stop trying to save the past and instead create the future: a high‑value, AI‑enabled, multilingual digital services hub for Africa, Europe, and the Indian Ocean. From Call Centres to Knowledge Centres Our call centres must evolve into AI‑enabled Customer Experience Centres , where Mauritian workers collaborate with digital assistants, multilingual platforms, and customer analytics. This transformation will protect jobs by shifting workers into higher‑skilled roles, ensuring that automation becomes a partner, not a threat. At the same time, Mauritius must move decisively up the value chain: Knowledge Process Outsourcing in finance, insurance, and legal services.
text_paragraph_2: These are the industries of tomorrow, and Mauritius must claim them today. Connecting Strategy to Jobs We already have the foundations: the Digital Transformation Blueprint 2025‑2029 , the National AI Strategy launched in 2026 , and government support for AI skill development. The challenge now is to connect these strategies directly to jobs, investments, and the survival and transformation of the BPO workforce. That is why we call for an Urgent BPO Workforce Transition Programme :

title: #VoteForHealthNaija: Turning Health Promises into Measurable Commitments Ahead of Nigeria’s 2027…
text_paragraph_1: Health continues to struggle to secure sufficient fiscal and political priority in Nigeria, and the gap between commitments, budget releases, and actual expenditure shows why. Nigeria’s 2026 federal budget allocated 3.7% to health, a figure far below the 15% budgetary target African leaders pledged under the 2001 Abuja Declaration . BudgIT’s 2025 State of States report found that only seven states, Yobe, Gombe, Ekiti, Lagos, Edo, Delta and Bauchi, spent more than 80% of their 2024 health budgets.
text_paragraph_2: The question, therefore, is what will it take for health to be given greater political priority? Once every four years, Nigerians go to the polls, giving political aspirants an opportunity to set out their commitments and explain what they intend to deliver if elected. In some countries, elections can be won or lost partly on the strength of aspirants’ competing health policies. Historically, that has not been the case in Nigeria. Health has rarely carried that level of political weight in Nigeria.
text_paragraph_3: As the 2027 election season approaches, the electoral window is opening for advocacy to push health higher up the political agenda. This means engaging citizens more actively and creating space for civil society and other stakeholders to define what they should expect from political aspirants, and the commitments against which those seeking office should ultimately be held accountable. With the 2027 elections in sight, Nigeria Health Watch convened a breakfast meeting themed “Health as a Political Issue: Driving Accountability and Citizen Engagement Ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 Elections.”

South Sudan’s vanishing forests: Communities must lead the fight to save them
text_paragraph_1: South Sudan is blessed with vast forests and woodlands that sustain millions of people and support some of the country’s most valuable ecosystems. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), South Sudan’s forests and woodlands cover approximately 191,667 square kilometers, representing about 30 percent of the country’s land area (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO], 2025). These forests provide timber, fuelwood, medicinal plants, and critical habitats for biodiversity (FAO, 2025; United Nations Environment Programme [UNEP], 2024).
text_paragraph_2: Yet despite their immense value, South Sudan’s forests are disappearing at an alarming rate. Annual forest loss has been estimated at between 1.5 and 2 percent, driven largely by fuelwood collection, charcoal production, agricultural expansion, livestock activities, and construction demands (UNEP, 2018, 2024). If this trend continues, the environmental and economic consequences could be severe for both present and future generations.
text_paragraph_3: The warning signs are increasingly visible across the country. Growing demand for charcoal, timber, and agricultural land is placing enormous pressure on forest resources. Urban centers, particularly Juba, consume vast quantities of charcoal and fuelwood. A UNEP-supported survey found that 88 percent of households in Juba rely on charcoal as their primary source of energy (UNEP, 2018). As forests shrink, communities become more vulnerable to environmental degradation, climate-related shocks, and declining natural resources (FAO, 2023; World Bank Group, 2026).

title: ITUC-Africa commends Togo over UN correct Africa map adoption
text_paragraph_1: ITUC-Africa has commended Togo for spearheading a United Nations resolution correcting Africa’s geographical representation.
text_paragraph_2: The African Regional Organisation of the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC-Africa) has commended Togo for spearheading a United Nations resolution correcting Africa’s geographical representation. Joel Odigie, the general secretary of ITUC-Africa, said this in a statement on Sunday. Mr Odigie said the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution promoting the Equal Earth map projection, which more accurately represents Africa’s geographical size and importance. He said the resolution, spearheaded by Togo and supported by the African Union, received overwhelming backing, with 164 UN member states voting for its adoption. According to him, Togo’s leadership demonstrated that African countries could influence global debates and institutions when they acted with unity, confidence, determination and clarity. “ITUC-Africa commends the government and people of Togo for the Pan-African spirit, determination and leadership demonstrated in advancing this historic and important initiative,” he said. Mr Odigie said the widespread use of the Mercator projection had, for centuries, visually diminished Africa while disproportionately enlarging parts of Europe and North America. He said the distortion went beyond cartography, noting that maps influenced education, public imagination, policymaking and perceptions of political and economic power. “Correcting this longstanding distortion is therefore an important act of historical and representational justice for Africa and its peoples,” he said. Mr Odigie said Africa’s true geographical size reflected its vast possibilities, including its growing population, strategic resources, productive capacity and expanding workforce. He said the development should serve as a clarion call for Africans to recognise their collective strengths and deploy them towards shared development and prosperity. The ITUC-Africa scribe said the African Continental Free Trade Area must move beyond agreements and declarations to deliver practical benefits for workers and ordinary Africans. “Africa needs greater regional integration, increased intra-African trade, improved infrastructure and freer, safer mobility for workers and people,” he said. He urged African governments to dismantle administrative, transport and financial barriers that continued to fragment economies and restrict cooperation among African peoples. Mr Odigie said correcting Africa’s geographical map should also compel Africans to examine ownership and control of land, minerals, energy, technology, finance and productive assets. He said inequality remained widespread despite Africa’s enormous wealth, while millions of workers faced unemployment, informality, inadequate wages and limited social protection. “The energy and unity demonstrated through the ‘Correct the Map’ campaign must now embolden a broader Pan-African agenda for structural transformation,” he said. He urged African leaders to diversify beyond raw material exports, build regional value chains and strengthen productive capacities under accountable and democratic stewardship. According to him, Africa’s true size must ultimately be reflected not only on global maps, but also in its influence and improved living standards. “Ordinary people must experience the dividends of African integration and transformation through decent work, living wages, universal social protection and quality public services,” he said. Mr Odigie congratulated Togo, the African Union and other stakeholders who championed the resolution, describing the achievement as a significant Pan-African victory. “Africa has been restored to its proper scale on the map. The greater task is ensuring its workers and peoples occupy their rightful place,” he said.

Tanzania Must Risk Becoming "Broke" to Create 20 Million Jobs
text_paragraph_1: Tanzania may need to accept less government revenue today to create far more economic activity tomorrow. With a tax-to-GDP ratio of just 12.8%, well below the 17-20% the country needs, and 71.8% of its workforce operating informally, Tanzania cannot tax its way to the revenue it wants from a formal economy this narrow. If the country seriously wants to generate 10 million to 20 million productive jobs over the next 20 years, it must rethink taxation, deregulation and investment incentives around one objective: expanding the productive economy fast enough to create millions of new taxpayers, businesses, workers and exporters.
text_paragraph_2: There is a dangerous idea in economic policy that Tanzania needs to collect more money from the economy before it can afford to create a better economy. The instinct is understandable, since government needs revenue to build roads, schools, hospitals, electricity networks, water systems and public institutions, and whenever revenue falls short, the natural response is to look for another tax, another levy, another fee, another compliance requirement or another activity that can be brought into the tax net. But there is a point at which this logic becomes self-defeating, because a government can become so focused on extracting revenue from the economy that it begins to reduce the very economic activity from which future revenue must come.
text_paragraph_3: Tanzania needs to consider the opposite proposition. If this country seriously wants to create between 10 million and 20 million additional productive jobs over the next 20 years, the government may have to accept collecting less money from some activities today in order to create a much larger economy tomorrow. That means deregulation, eliminating some taxes and levies, reducing the cost of formalisation, and allowing businesses in high-employment sectors to operate at margins that make expansion worthwhile. It means accepting that there will be years in which the government deliberately leaves money on the table because the private sector can generate a much greater economic return by retaining that money and investing it. In other words, Tanzania may need to risk becoming "broke" before it becomes rich, though that does not mean bankrupting the state. It means being willing to tolerate a temporary reduction in government revenue in carefully selected areas where every shilling left in the hands of producers has the potential to generate several shillings of new economic activity, wages, exports, investment and eventually taxable income.

title: Tanzania's $3.6 Trillion Dira 2050 Financing Plan, Explained
text_paragraph_1: Tanzania needs $3.6 trillion in cumulative investment between 2026 and 2050 to deliver Dira 2050 and reach a $1 trillion economy, according to the country's Long Term Perspective Plan and independent analysis by ODI. Seventy percent of that, roughly $2.5 trillion, is expected to come from private capital rather than government spending, a figure senior officials have called central to the plan rather than optional. Tanzania's own Minister of State for Planning and Investment has put the underlying logic bluntly: if a project can make money, why should taxpayers build it? The answer to that question, and whether Tanzania can actually build the institutions capable of attracting $2.5 trillion in private capital over 25 years, is what will determine whether Dira 2050 becomes a real economy or remains a planning document.
text_paragraph_2: DAR ES SALAAM — Tanzania has put a precise, and genuinely enormous, number on what Dira 2050 will actually cost: $3.6 trillion in cumulative investment between 2026 and 2050 to build a $1 trillion economy, according to the country's Long Term Perspective Plan, a figure independently confirmed by the ODI think tank's own analysis of the same planning assumptions. That's more than five times the size of Tanzania's projected economy at the start of the planning period, and it fundamentally changes what Dira 2050 is actually asking of the country. Tanzania isn't simply being asked to grow faster. It's being asked to mobilise private capital at a scale it has never previously approached, while simultaneously deepening domestic financial markets, attracting substantially more foreign investment, and building institutions capable of preparing projects that investors can actually finance.
text_paragraph_3: The Long Term Perspective Plan puts total investment requirements between 2026 and 2050 at approximately $3.6 trillion, though the exact figure varies slightly depending on the source and date, ODI's analysis independently arrives at roughly the same figure, while a March 2026 report from the Tanzania Investment and Consultant Group cites $3.7 trillion under similar assumptions. The requirement rises sharply across each of Tanzania's five-year development plans. One Region, Two Blocks: What Is The Future Of West Africa’s Regional Cooperation?
text_paragraph_1: The Liptako-Gourma Charter, signed in September 2023 as a mutual defence pact between Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger to provide collective security against terrorism and armed groups, took on a new form in January 2025 when these three frontier Sahelian states walked out of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). The Charter has evolved into the Alliance of Sahel States (Alliance des Etats du Sahel) and commands political and economic authority in the Sahel region.
text_paragraph_2: The walkaway, whilst celebrated in Bamako, Ouagadougou and Niamey, was unwelcomed in the corridors of the ECOWAS Commission in Abuja. An event of greater magnitude than a political disagreement transpired: the regional organisation experienced a loss of 54 percent of its geographical area, 17 percent of its inhabitants, and its entire northern border within a single day.
text_paragraph_3: Considering the fifty-year experiment of the regional block, this development has the semblance of an obituary, but it is not. Nonetheless, it would be misleading to claim that ECOWAS came out of this rift unscathed. The crucial question for all citizens, traders, students, and policymakers in the remaining twelve member nations is not whether ECOWAS has been harmed. It manifestly has, but how bad is it? In terms of land area, the three seceding states comprised 54 percent of the whole expanse of ECOWAS. The regional block now oversees a coastal and island community that has entirely relinquished its continental interior frontier — a geographic dismemberment that has immediate repercussions for the regional security structure.

The Sahel Blind Spot: How Russia’s ‘Africa Corps’ Outmaneuvered US Special Operations
text_paragraph_1: On August 5, 2024, the Pentagon completed the handover of Air Base 201—a facility near Agadez, Niger, built at a cost of roughly $110 million and once billed as the largest U.S. Air Force-led construction project in the service’s history—to Niger’s military junta. The drawdown had begun on May 19 under mutually agreed withdrawal conditions; Air Base 101 in Niamey was turned over on July 7. On September 16 the Defense Department declared the withdrawal complete, including the departure of the AFRICOM Coordination Element and its two-star general. A presence that had peaked near 1,000 personnel was gone in under four months.
text_paragraph_2: What came next is instructive—and should be studied carefully rather than simplified. The narrative that Russia’s Africa Corps simply walked into U.S. bases and plugged in their equipment requires factual correction. What happened is more complicated, and in some ways more troubling.
text_paragraph_3: The Russian military—operating through the rebranded Wagner Group network now formally designated Africa Corps and reportedly overseen by Russian military intelligence (GRU)—had already established a presence in Niger before U.S. forces completed their withdrawal. Then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin confirmed in May 2024, and the BBC reported at the time, that Russian troops were moved into a wing of Air Base 101 near Niamey while American personnel were still present at the facility. That specific, documented overlap—Russian forces occupying one section of a base while U.S. forces occupied another—is a remarkable data point about the speed of the strategic transition.
